extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and scholars of literature (especially those studying Toni Morrison, Black feminism, and postmodern fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the literary techniques, thematic commitments, and political perspectives by which Toni Morrison's works are evaluated — e.g., postmodern feminist features, Black feminist themes, narrative strategies, and audience/voice choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postmodern feminist characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Morrison exemplifies characteristics of 'postmodern feminism' by 'altering Euro-American dichotomies by rewriting a history written by mainstream historians' and by her usage of shifting narration in Beloved and Paradise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kottiswari (Postmodern Feminist Writers, 2008) — identify authors as postmodern feminist when they disrupt dominant Euro-American binaries, rewrite mainstream historical narratives from marginalized perspectives, and employ narrative strategies (e.g., shifting narration) that undermine singular authoritative voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage of shifting narration / multiple narrative voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of shifting narration (multiple perspectives and voices) as a formal technique in novels such as Beloved and Paradise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting narration functions to decentralize a single authoritative viewpoint, complicate linear history, and foreground communal or polyphonic memory; when evaluating fiction, look for scene-by-scene or chapter-by-chapter shifts that redistribute focalization among characters and collective subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-visionist approach to myth and folklore
rubrics_metrics.description: Morrison's approach to myth and folklore is 're-visionist' — she remakes, reinterprets, and reclaims traditional narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that rework myth/folklore to center marginalized subjects, to alter meanings of canonical stories, or to expose gaps in received mythologies can be read as re-visionist. Evaluate how the text re-signifies mythic material rather than simply alluding to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful, vivid language of women of color
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for 'the powerful vivid language of women of color' rather than 'western logocentric abstractions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prose for idiomatic, culturally rooted diction, imagery, and rhetorical patterns drawn from Black vernaculars, oral traditions, and community speech; such language use is treated as a deliberate aesthetic choice that privileges embodied, localized expression over abstracted Western theoretical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black feminist thematic commitments (lesbian perspective, autonomy, critique of conventional family)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works like Sula present a 'lesbian perspective that challenges heterosexual relationships and the conventional family unit' and 'poses both lesbian and feminist questions about Black women's autonomy and their impact upon each other's lives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a text contributes to Black feminist literature, look for thematic interrogation of heteronormativity, portrayals of intimate same-sex relationships or solidarities, explorations of Black women's agency/autonomy, and depictions of interpersonal dynamics that complicate normative family structures (as noted by Barbara Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing without the white gaze / centering African-American experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Morrison explicitly aimed to 'write without the gaze, without the white gaze,' centering African-American culture and people as the universe of concern rather than making work primarily about how white readers perceive Black lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts on whether they treat marginalized characters' inner lives and cultural worlds as intrinsic subjects rather than as objects for white validation; watch for narrative choices that resist framing Black experience through white perspectives or moralizing judgments aimed at white audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience: writing for Black women; repossessing and renaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Morrison stated 'I write for black women... Black women writers look at things in an unforgiving/loving way. They are writing to repossess, re-name, re-own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the voice, address, and cultural assumptions of a text: does it presume intimate knowledge shared among Black women, employ language/concerns that are reparative or recuperative, or enact forms of cultural reclamation (repossess, rename, re-own)? These are markers of commitment to a Black-woman-centered readership and project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the white male gaze as political/feminist stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Morrison 'consistently advocated for feminist ideas that challenge the dominance of the white patriarchal system,' rejecting the notion of writing from the perspective of the 'white male gaze.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authorial and narrative positions for explicit or implicit refusal to prioritize white patriarchal norms: does the work critique systems of racialized patriarchy, refuse to pander to expectations derived from those norms, or actively re-center marginalized perspectives as normative within the text?

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating expansive, 'universal' resonance from particular Black experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Zadie Smith described Morrison as having 'rejected the very concept of the narrow door and claimed for herself the wide world,' making Morrison 'as available to [every school child]—as 'universal'—as any other writer in the canon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating broader cultural impact or literary reach, note how a work rooted in particular cultural experience can articulate themes, emotions, or formal inventions that reach readers across backgrounds; universality here is produced by depth and imaginative range rather than erasure of particularity.
